subject: Astronomy & Space
title: New Horizons at Pluto
description: A fast breakdown of New Horizons at Pluto for builders.

hook.text: New Horizons traveled 5 billion km over 9 years to reach Pluto. The flyby lasted just one day.

buildup.text: Before 2015, the best images of Pluto were blurry smudges a few pixels wide.

discovery.text: It found ice mountains taller than the Rockies, nitrogen glaciers, and a vast heart-shaped plain.

twist.text: Pluto has a thin atmosphere that freezes and falls as snow when it drifts farther from the Sun.

climax.text: After Pluto, the probe flew past Arrokoth—a pristine, snowman-shaped rock from the early solar system.

punchline.text: Nine years of travel for one day at Pluto. Worth every km.

quiz.question: What surprising features did New Horizons discover on Pluto?
options: Ice mountains, nitrogen glaciers, and a heart-shaped plain
Active volcanoes and flowing lava rivers
Dense clouds and a thick nitrogen atmosphere

details.summary: NASA's New Horizons spacecraft flew past Pluto on July 14, 2015, after a 9.5-year journey, revealing a stunningly complex world: nitrogen glaciers, ice mountains taller than the Rockies, a thin atmosphere, and the heart-shaped Tombaugh Regio.
details.whyItMatters: New Horizons transformed Pluto from a blurry dot into a known world, showing that even small, distant bodies can be geologically active and complex. It overturned the assumption that objects far from the Sun are frozen, inert worlds.
takeaways: New Horizons revealed Pluto as a complex, geologically active world
It found nitrogen glaciers, ice mountains, and a thin atmosphere
The flyby took place in July 2015 after 9.5 years of travel

faq.question: What powers geological activity on Pluto?
faq.answer: Radioactive decay of elements in Pluto's rocky core likely provides enough heat to maintain a subsurface ocean of liquid water beneath the icy crust. Tidal interactions with Charon may contribute. This residual heat drives the nitrogen glacial flows and geological processes visible on the surface.

faq.question: Where is New Horizons now?
faq.answer: After Pluto, New Horizons flew past Arrokoth (formerly Ultima Thule) in the Kuiper Belt in 2019 — the most distant object ever visited. It's now heading deeper into the Kuiper Belt, still returning data about the outer solar system's environment. It has enough power to operate into the mid-2030s.
